In experiment 1, subjects had to decide which of two successively presented two-dot separations was wider. Over the range of interstimulus intervals employed (0 to 30 s), there was a linear relationship between interstimulus interval and spatial interval thresholds.<\/jats:p>\n                  <jats:p>In experiment 2 subjects' abilities to represent accurately more than one spatial interval at a time was investigated. Three dot pairs were presented, but only two pairs were to be compared, the third being completely irrelevant to the task. This manipulation doubled thresholds (relative to a two-dot-pair control condition), whether or not subjects were obliged to attend to the irrelevant dots. Overall, the results suggest that mental representations of spatial information may be temporally durable, but only in the absence of extraneous stimuli. The latter not only disrupt memory for spatial information, but appear to have obligatory access to it.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.1068\/p250053","type":"journal-article","created":{"date-parts":[[2007,1,23]],"date-time":"2007-01-23T10:32:54Z","timestamp":1169548374000},"page":"53-64","source":"Crossref","is-referenced-by-count":18,"title":["Decay
